tldr: Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates - XRG) won the Monaco opener, blew the race apart with a 50 km solo raid in Andorra on stage 4 and had three stage wins and a 3:50 lead when a heavy crash on stage 8 ended his Vuelta with a broken collarbone. Enric Mas (Movistar) inherited the red jersey, won the Alto de Aitana queen stage and leads Primož Roglič by 1:45 and Felix Gall by 2:06 after 13 stages, with Team Visma | Lease a Bike collecting four stage wins through Matthew Brennan (three) and Wout van Aert.

narrative.headline: Pogačar dominates, then crashes out; Mas inherits red and builds a lead over Roglič and Gall
narrative.openingMoves: The 2026 Vuelta a España began in Monaco with a short, technical 9.4 km individual time trial that Tadej Pogačar won by nine hundredths of a second over Ethan Hayter, taking the race's first red jersey. Grand Tour debutant Matthew Brennan won the uphill sprint in Manosque on stage 2 after Wout van Aert's late attack for the jersey was caught, and the first summit finish at Font-Romeu on stage 3 was cancelled mid-stage when a hailstorm hit the Col de Mont-Louis, with no winner declared.
narrative.raceUnfolds:
Stage 4 in Andorra was the race-defining day of the first week: Pogačar attacked alone on the Collada de Beixalis with 50 km to go, rode solo over the Coll d'Ordino and won by 2:39, opening a 3:21 overall lead on Primož Roglič. Brennan took a second sprint win on a windy Catalan stage 5, then Pogačar attacked on the gravel of the Puerto de Bartolo on stage 6, was caught by Enric Mas before the summit and beat him in a two-up sprint in Castelló for a third stage win. Andreas Leknessund led a Uno-X one-two at Aramón Valdelinares on stage 7 while Van Aert took the green jersey and Pogačar counter-attacked the GC group to stretch his lead over Mas to 3:50.

Stage 8 to Xeraco changed everything. Roughly 32 km from the finish, on the approach to the Puerto de Barx, Pogačar went down hard in a peloton crash that also caught Ben Tulett. He tried to remount but could not continue and left the race by ambulance with a concussion, a displaced collarbone fracture and a stable neck fracture, the first Grand Tour abandon of his career. Bryan Coquard out-sprinted Mads Pedersen for the stage, and Mas became race leader for the first time in his career, 1:00 ahead of Roglič and 1:11 ahead of Felix Gall.

Mas answered the pressure immediately, attacking inside the final 3 km of the Alto de Aitana queen stage on stage 9 to win and extend his lead to 1:18, with only Oscar Onley able to follow. After the rest day, Bastien Tronchon surprised the sprinters in Elche de la Sierra and Brennan completed a hat-trick in Lorca off a Van Aert lead-out, while Pedersen left the race with illness. On stage 12 Jakob Omrzel soloed to a breakthrough win on Calar Alto as Mas dropped Roglič and Gall on the final climb to push his lead to 1:45; Onley crashed early and slipped to fifth. Van Aert finally took his own stage on stage 13 into Loja, out-sprinting Valentin Paret-Peintre from a two-man move after Brennan neutralised the breakaway's attacks.
narrative.decision: Not yet decided. After 13 of 21 stages Enric Mas leads Primož Roglič by 1:45 and Felix Gall by 2:06, with Richard Carapaz (+3:53), Oscar Onley (+4:29) and Jakob Omrzel (+4:59) next. The Sierra de la Pandera summit finish, the Sierra Nevada mountains and the 32 km Jerez time trial are still to come.
narrative.finale: Not yet raced. The route continues through Andalusia before finishing in Madrid on 13 September.

decisiveMoments.headline: Pogačar wins the opening time trial by 0.09 seconds
decisiveMoments.description: On a technical, corner-heavy 9.4 km course through Monaco, Tadej Pogačar started second-to-last and edged out Ethan Hayter by nine hundredths of a second to take the stage and the race's first red jersey.

decisiveMoments.headline: Pogačar's 50 km solo raid blows the GC apart
decisiveMoments.description: Pogačar attacked on gradients of up to 16 percent with 50 km to go, rode alone over the Coll d'Ordino and won by 2:39 on the chasing group, turning a nine-second lead into a 3:21 advantage over Roglič after just four stages.

decisiveMoments.location: Approach to the Puerto de Barx (Stage 8)
decisiveMoments.headline: The race leader crashes out
decisiveMoments.description: A heavy peloton crash roughly 32 km from the finish in Xeraco left Pogačar with a concussion and a broken collarbone. He tried to remount but was withdrawn by ambulance, handing the red jersey to Enric Mas and resetting a race Pogačar had led by 3:50.

decisiveMoments.headline: Mas wins the queen stage in his first day in red
decisiveMoments.description: Rather than defend, Enric Mas attacked inside the final 3 km of the week-one queen stage, dropped every rival except Oscar Onley and took the stage to extend his lead to 1:18 over Roglič.

decisiveMoments.headline: Mas drops Roglič and Gall to push his lead past 1:45
decisiveMoments.description: On the final ramps of Calar Alto, Mas accelerated away from Roglič and Gall while Jakob Omrzel won the stage from the break, stretching the overall lead to 1:45 with the Sierra de la Pandera and Sierra Nevada still ahead.

riderPerformances.name: Tadej Pogačar
riderPerformances.narrative: Pogačar won the Monaco time trial, the 50 km Andorra raid on stage 4 and the gravel finale in Castelló on stage 6, and had stretched his overall lead to 3:50 by stage 7 in what was shaping up as a crushing first Vuelta victory. A heavy peloton crash on the flat run-in to Xeraco on stage 8 ended it: a concussion, a displaced collarbone fracture and a stable neck fracture forced the first Grand Tour abandon of his career. He had collarbone surgery on 31 August.

keyMoments.what: Stage 1: won the Monaco ITT by 0.09 seconds to take the race lead
Stage 4: 50 km solo attack from the Collada de Beixalis; won by 2:39 and opened a 3:21 GC lead
Stage 6: attacked on the Puerto de Bartolo gravel and beat Enric Mas in a two-up sprint for his third stage win
Stage 8: crashed heavily approaching the Puerto de Barx and abandoned with a broken collarbone

incident.detail: Stage 8: heavy peloton crash ~32 km from the finish; concussion, displaced left clavicle fracture and stable C7 fracture forced his withdrawal

riderPerformances.name: Primož Roglič
riderPerformances.narrative: Roglič conceded 22 seconds in the Monaco opener and 2:39 to Pogačar's Andorra raid, and was distanced again on the Bartolo gravel and at Valdelinares. Pogačar's abandon lifted him to second overall, but Enric Mas has since dropped him twice: on Aitana, where Roglič limited the damage to 12 seconds and took bonus seconds for third, and on Calar Alto, where the gap grew to 1:45.

keyMoments.what: Stage 9: third on Aitana, 12 seconds behind Mas, holding second overall
Stage 12: dropped by Mas on the final climb of Calar Alto; gap grows to 1:45

riderPerformances.name: Felix Gall
riderPerformances.narrative: Gall was the only rider able to follow Pogačar's first acceleration on the Beixalis and has been the most aggressive of the remaining contenders, attacking repeatedly on Valdelinares and Aitana with his Decathlon CMA CGM team setting the pace. He sits third at 2:06 but lost mountain lieutenant Gregor Mühlberger to an abandon on stage 13, days before the Sierra de la Pandera.

keyMoments.what: Stage 9: repeated attacks on Aitana moved him to third overall
Stage 12: dropped by Mas alongside Roglič on Calar Alto

riderPerformances.name: Richard Carapaz
riderPerformances.narrative: Carapaz led the chase over the Beixalis behind Pogačar but lost ground at Valdelinares, then bounced back on Aitana by attacking across to the breakaway remnants. He sits fourth overall at 3:53.

keyMoments.what: Stage 9: attacked from the GC group across to the break on Aitana

riderPerformances.name: Oscar Onley
riderPerformances.narrative: Onley followed the key moves on Beixalis and was the only rider to stay with Mas on the Alto de Aitana, finishing second on the queen stage and rising to fourth overall. An early crash on stage 12 compromised his day on Calar Alto and he slipped to fifth, still in the white jersey fight.

keyMoments.what: Stage 9: second on Aitana, the only rider to follow Mas
Stage 12: slid out on a roundabout, chased back, lost time on Calar Alto

incident.detail: Stage 12: slid out on a roundabout ~131 km from the finish; remounted and rejoined the peloton

riderPerformances.name: Mattias Skjelmose
riderPerformances.narrative: Skjelmose lost contact with the favourites on the closing climb in Andorra and shed more time on the Bartolo gravel and at Valdelinares, but has turned to the breakaway for GC gains: riding the stage 13 break into Loja clawed back roughly two minutes and lifted him to seventh overall at 5:32.

keyMoments.what: Stage 13: rode the day-long breakaway to gain around two minutes on the GC group

riderPerformances.name: Matthew Brennan
riderPerformances.narrative: The 21-year-old Grand Tour debutant has three stage wins: the uphill sprint in Manosque on stage 2, a led-out sprint on stage 5 and the reduced-bunch finish in Lorca on stage 11, each set up by Wout van Aert. On stage 13 he returned the favour, riding in the break and shutting down every attack so Van Aert could win.

keyMoments.what: Stage 2: won the uphill sprint in Manosque for his first Grand Tour stage win
Stage 5: second stage win from a Visma lead-out
Stage 11: hat-trick in Lorca off Van Aert's lead-out
Stage 13: neutralised the break so Van Aert could win

riderPerformances.name: Wout van Aert
riderPerformances.narrative: Van Aert attacked for the jersey on stage 2, took the green jersey with a day-long attack to third at Valdelinares on stage 7, and has led out Brennan's three sprint wins. On stage 13 he finally won his own Vuelta stage, out-sprinting Valentin Paret-Peintre in Loja from a two-man move; he leads the points classification ahead of Brennan.

keyMoments.what: Stage 2: attacked inside the final kilometre in a bid for the race lead
Stage 7: third from the day-long break; took the green jersey
Stage 13: first Vuelta stage win, beating Paret-Peintre in Loja

crashes.location: Stage 8, approach to the Puerto de Barx
crashes.description: Heavy peloton crash roughly 32 km from the finish at Xeraco, also involving Ben Tulett. Pogačar hit the tarmac hard, suffering a concussion, a displaced left collarbone fracture and a stable C7 vertebra fracture; he underwent collarbone surgery on 31 August.
Onley slid out on a roundabout about 131 km from the finish, remounted and chased back to the bunch, then lost further time on Calar Alto and dropped from fourth to fifth overall.

abandons.reason: Withdrawn by ambulance on stage 8 after a heavy crash with a suspected broken collarbone and a head injury while leading the race by 3:50 — the first Grand Tour abandon of his career.
Did not start stage 11 after withdrawing with illness.

aftermath.headline: Thirteen stages down, a race reset around Enric Mas
aftermath.body: As of the evening of 4 September 2026, after stage 13, Enric Mas leads the Vuelta a España by 1:45 over Primož Roglič and 2:06 over Felix Gall, with Richard Carapaz, Oscar Onley and Jakob Omrzel completing the top six. Tadej Pogačar, who had led by 3:50 with three stage wins, abandoned after a heavy crash on stage 8 and underwent collarbone surgery on 31 August; his team has not yet said whether he will race again this season. Wout van Aert leads the points classification from teammate Matthew Brennan. The race continues with the Sierra de la Pandera summit finish on stage 14 before the Sierra Nevada mountains, the Jerez time trial and the finish in Madrid on 13 September.
